one_liner: AMD's Zen-tuned replacements for glibc memcpy/memmove/memset/memcmp and str* functions, loaded by LD_PRELOAD or static link; no published speedups.
what_it_does: AOCL-LibMem (version 5.3.2) is a C library that exports the standard symbols memcpy, mempcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp, memchr, strcpy, strncpy, strcmp, strncmp, strlen, strnlen, strcat, strncat, strstr, strspn and strchr (strrchr is also implemented in the source), so it replaces glibc's versions with no code change when preloaded with LD_PRELOAD or linked ahead of libc as libaocl-libmem.a. The build picks one Zen generation (native detection, ALMEM_ARCH=zen1..zen6), one ISA (ALMEM_ISA=avx2|avx512), or runtime dispatch through IFUNC (ALMEM_DYN_DISPATCH=Y); a tunable build exposes LIBMEM_OPERATION and LIBMEM_THRESHOLD environment variables to force an instruction family, alignment variant or rep-movs/non-temporal thresholds.
how_it_is_fast: Size-tiered vector kernels: overlapping head/tail ZMM or YMM loads and stores for small sizes (up to 512 B on Zen4), then a destination-aligned 4- or 8-vector loop with software prefetch, rep movsb (ERMS) in a middle band on the AVX-512 optimised path, and non-temporal streaming stores above a threshold derived at load time from CPUID cache sizes (L2 per core, L3 per CCX). Per-microarchitecture variants (src/uarch/zen1..zen6) choose between these tiers and thresholds for each Zen generation, much like glibc's memmove-vec-unaligned-erms but with AMD-specific cut-offs.
when_to_use: Linux on AMD EPYC or Ryzen (Zen1 to Zen6) where profiles show memcpy/memmove/memset or str* time and you can test an LD_PRELOAD swap without rebuilding the application.
Fleet or HPC deployments already on the AOCL stack (AOCC, AOCL-BLIS, etc.) that want a matching libc string layer, built natively per node type or with IFUNC dispatch for mixed Zen fleets.
Copy-heavy workloads in the multi-KB to multi-MB range where Zen-specific rep-movsb and non-temporal thresholds can matter more than glibc's generic tunables.
When you are prepared to measure: the repo ships a harness (Google Benchmark hot/cold, tinymembench, FleetBench, DCPerf) that prints per-size throughput gain over the host glibc.
when_not_to_use: When you need published evidence: AMD gives no numbers in the README, User_Guide.md or benchmark_guide.md, so any gain over glibc must be measured on your own hardware.

Intel or non-x86 machines: the library is tuned and documented for Zen only; Linux only; an AVX-512 build crashes with illegal instructions on CPUs without AVX-512 (and the user guide warns behaviour is undefined if AVX-512 is disabled in BIOS on Zen4+).
Programs that hand a large memcpy result to another thread through a plain flag store: the Zen4 and AVX2 kernels stream non-temporal stores without a trailing sfence (see gotchas).

Builds that must run under strict memory checkers without extra configuration: the default build reads past the requested length inside the same page for small sizes; use ALMEM_STRICT_BOUNDS=Y for masked loads.
Portable binaries across glibc versions: a library built on glibc 2.34 or newer will not resolve its dlopen/dlsym symbols on older glibc.

integration.form: shared lib (libaocl-libmem.so via LD_PRELOAD) or static lib (libaocl-libmem.a linked before libc)
integration.dependencies: none at run time beyond glibc (2.34+ for the dynamic dispatcher build); building needs CMake 3.22 and GCC or AOCC; the benchmark tool needs Python 3.10+, numpy, pandas and Bazel below 8.0.0 for FleetBench
integration.min_toolchain: C99, CMake 3.22; GCC 14.1 for znver5 (newer GCC for znver6) or AOCC 5.0; IFUNC dispatch needs a recent toolchain
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 on AMD Zen1-Zen6; AVX2 or AVX-512 builds (AVX-512 build requires AVX-512 hardware)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the functions keep no mutable state after the load-time constructor sets thresholds and cache sizes (read in source)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — symbol-compatible drop-in for the 17 listed functions (plus strrchr in source) via LD_PRELOAD or static linking; every other libc function stays glibc's, and tunable variants such as LIBMEM_OPERATION=erms,w,w or avx2,y,y can corrupt data or crash on lengths or alignments they do not support

gotchas: Missing store fence (read in source, not reported in issues): src/uarch/zen4/memcpy_impl_zen4.c and src/isa/avx2/optimized/memcpy_avx2.c (the Zen3 variant) switch to non-temporal streaming stores at or above __nt_start_threshold and return without an sfence, while the AVX-512 optimised path (Zen5) issues ALM_STORE_FENCE() after its streaming loop and glibc does the same; NT stores are weakly ordered on x86, so a later plain store (e.g. a release flag) can become visible before the copied data.

CPU detection bug: RDSEED is tested in CPUID leaf 7 ECX bit 18 (src/cpu_features.c and the IFUNC resolver in src/libmem_ifunc_dispatcher.c) instead of EBX bit 18, so a dynamic-dispatch build on Zen1 (no RDPID, no VPCLMULQDQ) falls through to the generic 'system' variant instead of the zen1 kernels; GCC 16+ builds avoid it by using __builtin_cpu_is.

Vendor gating is inconsistent: the constructor computes cache sizes and thresholds only on AuthenticAMD, but the GCC<16 IFUNC resolver has no vendor check, so on Intel CPUs with AVX-512 it selects zen4/zen5/zen6 kernels running with unset (0 and 0xffffffff) cache sizes and thresholds.

Harness asymmetry in the shipped benchmark: with -preload n the LibMem binary links libaocl-libmem.a statically while the 'glibc' binary is still dynamically linked to libc (only -static-libgcc -static-libstdc++), so glibc pays PLT/IFUNC call overhead the LibMem arm does not; the default -preload y runs one binary both ways and is the fair mode. Both GBM drivers (gbm.py behind the documented bench.py, and new_gbm.py behind the redesigned benchmark.py) share that asymmetry; gbm.py also compiles the benchmark with no -O flag, new_gbm.py with -O3. README's note that ALMEM_ARCH selects AVX2/AVX512 is stale: BUILD_RUN.md and CMake use ALMEM_ISA for that and ALMEM_ARCH for zen1..zen6.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over asmlib (generic x86, numbers from glibc 2.7/2.8 era) or DPDK rte_memcpy (inline memcpy for small cached copies only) when you run Linux on AMD Zen and want a maintained, symbol-compatible LD_PRELOAD replacement for the whole mem*/str* set with per-Zen thresholds; Arm Optimized Routines is the counterpart for Arm and is not an alternative on x86.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing has been measured publicly: the repo only provides a harness whose default report times the host glibc against LibMem (LD_PRELOAD on one Google Benchmark binary, best of three runs with -bestperf) and prints throughput gain as (LibMem - glibc) / glibc in percent per size. The claim 'highly optimized for AMD Zen' is AMD's own and carries no hardware, compiler or numbers.
status_note: Maintained by AMD as part of AOCL (one squashed commit per release, 4.2 through 5.3.2 on 2026-08-20, 1 open issue, no GitHub releases or tags), BSD-3-Clause with bundled MIT tinymembench, small enough to vendor, but evidence is tier D until someone publishes runs of the shipped harness.
